html:
In 1692 and 1693 the Puritan colony of Massachusetts tried more than 200 people for witchcraft, starting in Salem Village. Nineteen were hanged, one man was pressed to death with stones, and several died in jail.

It began when girls in the house of the minister Samuel Parris had fits and accused his enslaved servant Tituba, later the heroine of a novel by Maryse Conde, and two other women. Accusations spread, and a special court accepted "spectral evidence", dreams and visions of the accused.

Doubts grew among ministers, and the governor ended the trials in 1693. Jurors and a judge later apologised, and the colony paid compensation. The trials, a late echo of the European witch hunts, became a symbol of fear and injustice, as in Arthur Miller's play The Crucible. They took place among the heirs of the Puritan migration.
